data.text:
Happy birthday, Warren Buffett!​
​
Warren turns 96 this month and I’ve been thinking about how to sum up almost 35 years of our friendship. ​
​
It was a deep friendship from our very first conversation. And I’ve never stopped learning from him since. I think his jokes are all funny. His dietary habits are excellent. He once told me he looked at the data and figured out that first graders have the best actuarial odds, so he decided to eat like one. He was only half joking. ​
​
He’s gifted at investing in people. Warren has always found time to nurture friendships like few other people I know. He’s one of the most patient people I’ve ever met. I’m still amazed by his ability to draw people in and he makes it fun to learn from him. ​
​
He sticks to what he believes in. I once wrote him a letter about the example he set by sticking to what he believes in. That’s stuck with me for all these years. ​
​
We never run out of things to talk or laugh about. And if there’s one thing Warren has taught me, it’s what friendship is really all about. In short, I’m a fan. ​
​
Happy 96th birthday, my friend.​

poster.headline: Chair, Gates Foundation and Founder, Breakthrough Energy

data.text:
The world needs a plan to ensure that AI’s benefits outweigh the harm it causes, and we need to start now. It’s a monumental challenge that requires us to create new domestic and international organizations, create protections for workers, change our tax code, and much more. Our plan needs to be shaped by people whose voices aren’t often heard in this kind of discussion, including workers, college students, community leaders, religious leaders, parents, and educators. ​
​
If we get it right, the payoff for humanity will be phenomenal and the world will be a more equitable place:

data.article_title: The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical.

poster.headline: Chair, Gates Foundation and Founder, Breakthrough Energy

data.text:
AI will either be the greatest equalizer ever invented, or the worst source of injustice. Even under the best circumstances, the transition to this new AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history. How will we use this technology to make the world a fairer place and keep it from widening the divide between rich and poor? How will we protect the people who are most vulnerable to the harms caused by artificial intelligence, including those who lose their livelihoods and the sense that they are in control of their future?

Answering these questions and acting on the answers should be the world’s top priority. If the world takes the right steps, AI will be a force for good and leave everyone better off.

data.resharer_comment: Advances in blood biomarkers have already helped accelerate Alzheimer’s research, and this partnership could take those insights even deeper. Making the dataset broadly available will also give researchers across the field the opportunity to build on those findings and push the science further.
data.text:
We’re expanding a partnership with Alamar Biosciences, Inc., supported by Gates Ventures, to add multiplex protein profiling of 80,000+ additional plasma samples to the NULISA NeuroData Commons – a 2025 initiative that has already profiled more than 40,000 biosamples. The combined dataset is projected to represent the largest population-scale study of neurodegenerative disease. 
 
The additional samples will be profiled with Alamar’s newest neurology panel, NULISAseq™ Neuro 220. By measuring 220 biomarkers from a small blood or CSF sample, including eMTBR-Tau, the panel enables simultaneous blood-based capture of both hallmark Alzheimer's pathologies alongside p-Tau217 for the first time. 
 
The goal is to help enable researchers to understand how Alzheimer’s differs from person to person and use that to change how we treat and prevent it. Data will be shared with the global research community through AD Workbench, the same secure infrastructure leveraged by the Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium. 
 
Read the full announcement: https://lnkd.in/ezTfSZ-Y

X1 is proving out the technology for Heart's ES-30 regional airliner, which has customer commitments from United Airlines and Air Canada. Sometimes, when I tell people I’m optimistic about the future, they’re skeptical. How can I say that when so much seems to be going wrong in the world? ​
​
I see all these problems too, but through my work with the Gates Foundation and other organizations, I also get to witness proof of progress that helps me stay optimistic. ​
​
For example, in the past 50 years, childhood vaccines have saved 154 million lives; child mortality has fallen by more than half since 2000; and, for the first time ever, we have a blood test to detect Alzheimer’s disease and drugs that may slow its progress. ​
​
I love these facts and stats—not just because they’re impressive, but because they represent real people whose lives have been transformed thanks to the hard work of scientists, health workers, and countless others.

data.article_title: Heineken Is Trying a Heat Battery to Generate Steam for Its Brewing
data.resharer_comment: I’ll raise a glass for lower emissions.
data.text:
Brewing beer takes a lot of heat. And at its Portugal brewery, The HEINEKEN Company is testing a new way to supply it using Rondo Energy heat batteries to store wind and solar power in clay bricks at up to 1,500°C. That heat is then used to generate steam for brewing and pasteurization.

Industrial heat is a major energy challenge because factories need dependable heat at the exact moment when their processes require it. Thermal batteries give manufacturers an alternative: using clean electricity when it’s available and delivering stored heat back into the plant when needed.

Companies like Rondo, Antora Energy, and Tempo Innovations in our portfolio are building for that industrial reality with better approaches that are competitive on cost, reliable when production needs it, and clean.

data.text: I had the most incredible week in Rwanda. It was inspiring to hear from the next generation of leaders. Rwanda has already achieved remarkable progress with even greater opportunities ahead, and its young people are poised to shape not only the African continent, but the world.

data.resharer_comment: It was wonderful to learn from the next generation of leaders at the University of Global Health Equity. Building on my friend Paul Farmer’s vision of health equity, institutions like UGHE are helping train the next generation of doctors and public health leaders to strengthen the health systems their communities rely on, while networks like COMS-A are helping elevate these ideas across the continent.
data.text:
At the inaugural Paul E. Farmer #ButaroDialogues on Health Equity and Innovation, Mr. Bill Gates reflected on the legacy of Paul Farmer, whose vision and commitment continue to shape the work and spirit of Butaro. 

Recalling his journey with Dr. Paul, including visits to health facilities such as Rwinkwavu Hospital, Mr. Gates paid tribute to Dr. Paul’s enduring belief that “where you live should never determine whether you live.” He described UGHE as a testament to what Paul believed was possible and shared that, while he deeply misses Paul, it is comforting to see his legacy continue here in Butaro. 

In his lecture, Mr. Gates also recognized Rwanda’s remarkable progress in strengthening health systems, including significant reductions in child mortality and maternal deaths. He commended the country’s leadership in healthcare innovation and highlighted the importance of working together to ensure that proven solutions reach the people who need them most. 

“It is not a mystery what we need to do. We understand the challenge, and we have the tools to act.” 

Acknowledging that the world is facing a difficult period for global health, he noted that leaders must find ways to achieve more with fewer resources. He also warned that emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, must not become concentrated in wealthier countries or benefit only those who already have access. 

“AI should not only be available to those who already have access; we should bring AI to those who need it most.” 

Mr. Gates commended #UGHE’s One Health approach to making health more equitable and highlighted The Consortium of Medical Schools-Africa (COMS-A) as an important platform bringing medical schools together for better outcomes. He emphasized that institutions like UGHE can play a critical role in ensuring that innovation is developed, taught, and implemented equitably, helping transform health systems and expand access to life-saving solutions.

#HealthEquity #HealthInnovation
